questions.question_text: When a market is in equilibrium, the buyers are those with the _______ willingness to pay and the sellers are those with the ___________ costs
questions.explanation:
In equilibrium, the market clears at price $P^*$ where QD = QS.

Buyers side: Only buyers with Willingness to Pay $\geq P^*$ purchase the good. These are the buyers with the highest WTP — they value the good most and are willing to pay at least the market price.

Sellers side: Only sellers with Cost $\leq P^*$ find it profitable to sell. These are the sellers with the lowest costs — they are the most efficient producers.

This dual condition ensures all mutually beneficial trades are realized and Total Surplus is maximized.

questions.question_text: An increase in the supply of a good (that is, supply curve shifting right) will decrease the total revenue producers receive if
questions.explanation:
When supply shifts right, the equilibrium price falls and quantity rises. The net effect on Total Revenue (TR = P $\times$ Q) depends on the price elasticity of demand.

Case 1 — Inelastic demand (|PED| < 1): The percentage fall in price exceeds the percentage rise in quantity sold. The price effect dominates, so TR falls.

Case 2 — Elastic demand (|PED| > 1): The percentage rise in quantity exceeds the percentage fall in price. The quantity effect dominates, so TR rises.

Conclusion: An increase in supply decreases total producer revenue when demand is inelastic (Option A).

questions.question_text: The own price elasticity of demand at the current market equilibrium for cigarettes is (or the absolute value of the own price elasticity of demand for cigarettes is 0.5). As for the own price elasticity of supply at the current market equilibrium, it is . If a specific tax (per unit tax) is levied on producers, then

options.A: producers will bear a larger burden of the tax
options.B: consumers and producers will bear equal burden of the tax
options.C: consumers will bear a larger burden of the tax

questions.explanation:
Tax incidence depends on the relative elasticities of supply and demand. The more inelastic side of the market bears the larger share of the tax.

Given: |PED| = 0.5 (demand is inelastic — cigarettes are addictive necessities with no close substitutes).

Consumer's share of tax $\approx \frac{E_S}{E_S + |E_D|}$.

When supply is relatively more elastic than demand (|PES| > |PED| = 0.5), the consumer's share is larger.

Intuitively: inelastic demand means consumers cannot easily reduce cigarette purchases even as prices rise, so producers can pass most of the tax on to consumers.

Conclusion: Consumers bear the larger burden of the tax.

questions.question_text: Microeconomics by Pindyck and Rubinfeld is a textbook bought by only two types of students: MBA students and advanced undergraduates. The demand curve for MBA students is Qm=10 - P, where Qm is in thousands and is P in hundreds of rupees. The demand curve for advanced undergraduates is Qa=20 - 4P, where Qa is in thousands and P in hundreds of rupees.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: The total quantity demanded at a price Rs. 700 will be
questions.explanation:
Since P is measured in hundreds of rupees, convert the price: P = $\frac{700}{100}$ = 7.

Step 1: Calculate MBA demand at P = 7.
$Q_m$ = 10 - 7 = 3 (thousands) = 3,000 units.

Step 2: Calculate undergraduate demand at P = 7.
$Q_a$ = 20 - 4(7) = 20 - 28 = -8.
Since quantity demanded cannot be negative, $Q_a$ = 0. (Undergraduates are fully priced out when P > 5, i.e., when the price exceeds Rs 500.)

Step 3: Total quantity demanded.
$Q_{total}$ = 3,000 + 0 = 3,000 units.

questions.question_text: At price Rs.100, which of the following is correct

options.A: MBA demand is more elastic than the market demand
options.B: MBA demand is equally elastic as the market demand
options.C: MBA demand is less elastic than the market demand

questions.explanation:
Convert price: P = $\frac{100}{100}$ = 1.

Step 1: MBA elasticity at P = 1.
$Q_m$ = 10 - 1 = 9 (thousands).
$\varepsilon_m$ = $\left|\frac{dQ_m}{dP}\right| \times \frac{P}{Q_m}$ = 1 $\times \frac{1}{9} \approx$ 0.111.

Step 2: Market demand at P = 1 (since P = 1 < 5, both types buy).
$Q_{total}$ = (10 - P) + (20 - 4P) = 30 - 5P = 30 - 5(1) = 25 (thousands).
$\varepsilon_{market}$ = $\left|\frac{dQ}{dP}\right| \times \frac{P}{Q}$ = 5 $\times \frac{1}{25}$ = 0.200.

Step 3: Compare elasticities.
$\varepsilon_m$ = 0.111 < $\varepsilon_{market}$ = 0.200.

MBA demand is less elastic than market demand at P = Rs 100.

questions.question_text:
Let there be three types of consumers: High, Medium, and Low. Banana, a software company has a product called Pro-Max, which is produced at zero marginal cost. Also assume that there are 50 High type, 30 Medium type, and 20 Low type consumers. Moreover, each consumer has a demand for only one unit of Pro-Max. Following are the maximum willingness to pay for the product by the three consumers' types:

High: 120;         Medium: 60;         Low: 20.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: The uniform price (or a single price) that gives Banana, the highest revenue is
questions.explanation:
Since MC = 0, revenue equals profit. Evaluate revenue at each possible uniform price:

At P = 120: Only High types buy (WTP $\geq$ 120).
TR = 120 $\times$ 50 = 6,000.

At P = 60: High and Medium types buy (WTP $\geq$ 60).
TR = 60 $\times$ (50 + 30) = 60 $\times$ 80 = 4,800.

At P = 20: All types buy.
TR = 20 $\times$ (50 + 30 + 20) = 20 $\times$ 100 = 2,000.

Revenue is maximized at P = 120 with TR = 6,000.

questions.question_text: If Banana wants to price discriminate between the three types of consumers using price discrimination, then which of the following condition is not necessary

options.B: High type and Medium type consumers should not be able to arbitrage the price difference
options.C: High type and Low type consumers should not be able to arbitrage the price difference
options.D: Marginal cost of production has to be zero

questions.explanation:
Price discrimination requires exactly three conditions:
1. Market power: The firm must be able to set prices above marginal cost.
2. Market segmentation: The firm must identify and separate consumer types by their WTP.
3. No arbitrage: Consumers in lower-price segments cannot resell the good to those in higher-price segments.

Zero marginal cost is not a necessary condition. Price discrimination can be practiced at any MC level — the profit motive exists regardless of whether costs are zero or positive.

Option D (MC = 0) is the condition that is NOT necessary.

questions.question_text: Suppose Banana can observe characteristics that distinguish High type consumers from Medium and Low type consumers, but it can not distinguish between Medium and Low types consumers. Under these circumstances, what would be the revenue-maximizing prices that Banana should charge to the three types of consumers?

options.A: 120 to High type, 60 to Medium, and 20 to Low type
options.B: 60 to High type, 60 to Medium, and 20 to Low type
options.C: 120 to High type, 60 to Medium, and 60 to Low type
options.D: 120 to High type, 20 to Medium, and 20 to Low type

questions.explanation:
The firm can identify High types but cannot distinguish Medium from Low types.

For High types (50 consumers, WTP = 120):
Charge P = 120 (their full WTP). Revenue = 120 $\times$ 50 = 6,000.

For the indistinguishable Medium + Low group (30 + 20 = 50 consumers):
- At P = 60: Only Medium types buy (WTP $\geq$ 60). Revenue = 60 $\times$ 30 = 1,800.
- At P = 20: Both Medium and Low types buy. Revenue = 20 $\times$ 50 = 1,000.

Charging P = 60 to the entire group maximizes revenue from this segment (1,800 > 1,000).

Revenue-maximizing prices: 120 to High, 60 to Medium, and 60 to Low types.

questions.question_text: In a competitive market with (i) a large number of price-taking buyers and sellers, and (ii) a downward sloping linear market demand curve and an upward-sloping linear market supply curve, a market equilibrium
questions.explanation:
At the competitive market equilibrium ($P^*, Q^*$):
- All buyers with WTP $\geq P^*$ purchase the good (goods go to those who value them most).
- All sellers with cost $\leq P^*$ produce (production by the most efficient firms).
- All mutually beneficial trades are realized — no profitable trade is left unexploited.

Total Surplus = CS + PS = Value to buyers - Cost to sellers.

At equilibrium, no reallocation can make one party better off without making another worse off (Pareto efficiency). Therefore, Total Surplus is maximized at the competitive equilibrium.

questions.question_text: Let the market supply curve of alcoholic drinks be given by Qs = -4/3 + 4/3 P and the market price be P = 4 per alcoholic drink. What is the producer surplus?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Find the minimum supply price (price at which $Q_S$ = 0).
0 = -$\frac{4}{3}$ + $\frac{4}{3}P \Rightarrow \frac{4}{3}P$ = $\frac{4}{3} \Rightarrow P_{min}$ = 1.

Step 2: Find quantity supplied at P = 4.
$Q_S$ = -$\frac{4}{3}$ + $\frac{4}{3}(4)$ = -$\frac{4}{3}$ + $\frac{16}{3}$ = $\frac{12}{3}$ = 4.

Step 3: Calculate Producer Surplus (area of the triangle below the price and above the supply curve).
PS = $\frac{1}{2} \times$ (P - $P_{min}) \times$ Q = $\frac{1}{2} \times$ (4 - 1) $\times$ 4 = $\frac{1}{2} \times$ 3 $\times$ 4 = 6.

questions.question_text: Suppose the current equilibrium quantity of alcoholic beverages is Q* and the current equilibrium price is P*. The government wishes to reduce the quantity of alcoholic beverages sold, and therefore, is considering the imposition of a specific tax (on per unit of quantity sold) on the sellers of alcoholic drinks. Suppose that the market for alcoholic drinks can be described by (i) a large number of price-taking buyers and sellers of alcoholic drinks, and (ii) a downward sloping linear market demand curve and an upward sloping linear market supply curve.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: From the options given below, the reduction in the quantity sold of the alcohol in the market would be highest after the introduction of the tax when

options.A: market supply curve is inelastic at (P*,Q*), and the market demand curve is elastic at (P*,Q*)
options.B: both market supply and market demand curves are elastic at (P*,Q*)
options.C: both market supply and market demand curves are inelastic at (P*,Q*)
options.D: market supply curve is elastic at (P*,Q*) and the market demand curve is inelastic at (P*,Q*)

questions.explanation:
A per-unit tax drives a wedge between the buyer's price and the seller's price, reducing equilibrium quantity.

The reduction in quantity is larger when both sides respond strongly to price changes:
- Elastic supply: Sellers sharply reduce quantity when the net price they receive falls.
- Elastic demand: Buyers sharply reduce quantity when the price they pay rises.

When both supply and demand are elastic, the reduction in quantity traded from either side is large, so the combined fall in equilibrium quantity is maximized.

Conclusion: The quantity reduction is highest when both supply and demand are elastic (Option B).

questions.question_text: From the options given below, sellers of alcoholic drinks will bear the largest burden of the tax when

options.A: market supply curve is relatively inelastic compared to the market demand curve at (P*,Q*)
options.B: market supply curve is relatively elastic compared to the market demand curve at (P*,Q*)
options.C: market demand curve is perfectly inelastic
options.D: market supply curve is perfectly elastic

questions.explanation:
The tax burden falls more heavily on the more inelastic side of the market.

Seller's share of tax $\approx \frac{|E_D|}{E_S + |E_D|}$.

If supply is relatively more inelastic than demand ($E_S < |E_D|$): Sellers have fewer alternatives — they cannot easily shift production to other goods when their net price falls. They absorb a larger share of the tax through a lower net price received.

Option A (supply more inelastic than demand) means sellers bear the larger burden.

Note: Options C and D describe conditions where consumers bear most of the burden (perfectly inelastic demand or perfectly elastic supply).

questions.question_text: The average total cost to produce 100 cookies is \$0.25 per cookie. The marginal cost is constant at \$0.10 for all levels of cookies produced.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: The total cost to produce 50 cookies is:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Find Total Cost at Q = 100.
TC(100) = ATC $\times$ Q = 0.25 $\times$ 100 = \$25.

Step 2: Find Total Variable Cost at Q = 100 (since MC is constant, TVC = MC $\times$ Q).
TVC(100) = 0.10 $\times$ 100 = \$10.

Step 3: Solve for Fixed Cost.
FC = TC - TVC = 25 - 10 = \$15.

Step 4: Find Total Cost at Q = 50.
TC(50) = FC + MC $\times$ Q = 15 + 0.10 $\times$ 50 = 15 + 5 = \$20.

questions.question_text: At the level of 50 and 100 cookies, the average total cost is
questions.explanation:
From Q16, FC = \$15. The ATC function is:
ATC(Q) = $\frac{FC}{Q}$ + MC = $\frac{15}{Q}$ + 0.10.

At Q = 50: ATC = $\frac{15}{50}$ + 0.10 = 0.30 + 0.10 = \$0.40.
At Q = 100: ATC = $\frac{15}{100}$ + 0.10 = 0.15 + 0.10 = \$0.25.

As Q increases, $\frac{15}{Q}$ decreases, so ATC is always falling.

Key rule: When MC < ATC, the ATC curve is falling. Here MC = \$0.10 is always below ATC at both output levels, so ATC is falling at both Q = 50 and Q = 100.

questions.question_text:
Observe the following two statements regarding a cost function which must have a fixed cost:
I. The average total cost curve and the average variable cost curve reach their minima at the same level of output.
II. The average total cost curve and the marginal cost curve reach their minima at the same level of output.

options.A: Both I and II are true
options.B: Both I and II are false
options.C: I is true, and II is false
options.D: I is false, and II is true

questions.explanation:
Statement I: ATC and AVC reach their minima at the same output level?
ATC = AVC + AFC. Since AFC = FC/Q is always declining, ATC > AVC at every Q > 0. The MC curve crosses AVC at AVC's minimum and then crosses ATC at ATC's minimum (at a higher Q). ATC and AVC minima occur at different output levels. Statement I is FALSE.

Statement II: ATC and MC reach their minima at the same output level?
The MC curve has its own minimum (the point of diminishing returns), which occurs at a lower output than where MC crosses ATC (ATC's minimum). The MC and ATC curves share an intersection point (ATC's minimum), but the MC curve's own minimum is at a different, lower output level. Statement II is FALSE.

Both I and II are false.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT true for a monopoly facing a downward sloping linear demand curve?

options.A: The profit maximizing output is the one at which marginal revenue and marginal cost are equal
options.C: The monopolist's demand curve is the same as the market demand curve
options.D: At the profit maximizing output, price equals marginal cost

questions.explanation:
Evaluate each statement:

A (True): Profit maximization always requires MR = MC — this holds for all market structures.

B (True): $AR = \frac{TR}{Q} = \frac{P \times Q}{Q} = P$. Average revenue always equals price.

C (True): A monopolist is the sole seller, so it faces the entire downward-sloping market demand curve.

D (False): At the monopolist's profit-maximizing output, MR = MC, and the price is set above MC using the demand curve. For a monopolist, P > MR = MC. Setting P = MC is the condition for a perfectly competitive market, not a monopoly.

The statement that is NOT true is D.

questions.question_text: The figure below shows three different demand and supply graphs. Which graph best represents the market for vacation on planet Mars today?
questions.explanation:
Today, no technology exists to travel to or vacation on Mars. This means no seller can supply Mars vacations at any commercially viable price.

In market terms: the minimum price sellers would require to supply even one unit far exceeds the maximum price any consumer is willing to pay.

Graph A represents this situation — the supply curve lies entirely above the demand curve at every quantity. The two curves never intersect, so there is no equilibrium and zero quantity is traded.

This is a market that does not exist (yet).

questions.question_text: Along a downward sloping linear demand curve, total revenue is maximized:

options.A: where the elasticity is –1 (or the absolute value of the own price elasticity of demand is 1)
options.B: on the quantity axis intercept (that is, the point where demand curve meets the X-axis)

questions.explanation:
Total Revenue TR = P $\times$ Q. Along a linear demand curve:
- On the upper half (elastic portion, |PED| > 1): lowering price increases TR (quantity rises more than price falls).
- On the lower half (inelastic portion, |PED| < 1): raising price increases TR (price rises more than quantity falls).

TR is maximized exactly at the midpoint of the demand curve, where |PED| = 1 (unit elastic). This is also the point where Marginal Revenue = 0 (since MR = 0 is the condition for maximum TR).

At the quantity-axis intercept, P = 0, so TR = 0. At the price-axis intercept, Q = 0, so TR = 0. Both endpoints give TR = 0.

questions.question_text: Growers expect that the price of a bushel of wheat will increase in the coming month. This belief results in

options.A: an increase in current supply of wheat
options.B: a decrease in current supply of wheat
options.C: a decrease in future supply of wheat
options.D: no change in current or future supply of wheat

questions.explanation:
If growers expect the price of wheat to be higher next month, they have a profit incentive to withhold current supply — storing goods or delaying harvesting — to sell at the higher future price.

This reduces the quantity available in the current period, causing the current supply curve to shift leftward (decrease in current supply).

Result: current supply decreases.

questions.question_text: If the price of both a substitute and a complement for commodity X increases, the demand for X will:

options.D: Any of the above, depending on the situation

questions.explanation:
Trace the two simultaneous effects on demand for good X:

Effect 1 — Substitute's price rises: The substitute becomes relatively more expensive. Consumers switch away from the substitute toward X. Demand for X increases (shift right).

Effect 2 — Complement's price rises: The complement is now more costly. Consumers buy less of the complement, reducing their need for X as well. Demand for X decreases (shift left).

The two effects operate in opposite directions. The net outcome depends on which effect is stronger:
- If substitute effect > complement effect: Demand for X increases.
- If complement effect > substitute effect: Demand for X decreases.
- If both effects are exactly equal: Demand for X is unchanged.

Answer: any of the above outcomes is possible (Option D).

questions.question_text: If a firm employs some workers who can be dismissed at any time without pay, while others have contracts guaranteeing pay, the total wages and salaries paid by the firm are considered:

options.C: Partly a fixed cost and partly a variable cost

questions.explanation:
The firm has two types of workers with different cost structures:

Type 1 — Contract workers (guaranteed pay): The firm is contractually obligated to pay these wages regardless of output produced. These wages do not vary with production — they are a fixed cost.

Type 2 — Workers dismissible at any time: The firm only pays these workers when they are needed for production. As output rises, more are hired; as output falls, they are let go. These wages vary with output — they are a variable cost.

Since total wages include both types, total wages and salaries are partly a fixed cost and partly a variable cost.

questions.question_text: A firm is incurring losses but can still cover its variable costs, in the short-run it should:

options.A: Shut down immediately to avoid further losses
options.B: Continue producing in the short run to minimize losses
options.C: Stop production immediately due to losses

questions.explanation:
In the short run, fixed costs must be paid regardless of whether the firm produces or shuts down.

Shutdown rule: Shut down only if P < AVC (i.e., the firm cannot even cover its variable costs).

If P $\geq$ AVC (variable costs are fully covered):
- By producing: the firm pays all variable costs and uses the remaining revenue to partially offset fixed costs, reducing its total loss.
- By shutting down: the firm earns zero revenue but still pays all fixed costs — a larger loss.

Formally: Loss from producing = FC - (TR - TVC). Since TR $\geq$ TVC, this loss is less than FC (the shutdown loss).

Conclusion: The firm minimizes its loss by continuing to produce in the short run.

questions.question_text: On a linear demand curve, the lower the price
questions.explanation:
For a linear inverse demand curve P = A - BQ, the price elasticity of demand at any point (P, Q) is:
|PED| = $\frac{1}{B} \times \frac{P}{Q}.$

As we move down the demand curve:
- P decreases (numerator falls).
- Q increases (denominator rises).
- The ratio $\frac{P}{Q}$ decreases.

Therefore, |PED| decreases as price falls.

Interpretation: At low prices, the base is small relative to the absolute price change, so a given price cut represents a smaller percentage change, making demand less responsive (less elastic).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about a price ceiling is false?

options.A: Effective price ceiling decreases producer surplus
options.B: Effective price ceiling creates an excess demand
options.C: Effective price ceiling creates an excess supply
options.D: To have any effect, the price ceiling must be set at a lower level than the original equilibrium price.

questions.explanation:
A binding (effective) price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price: $P_C < P^*$.

Statement A (True): At $P_C < P^*$, sellers receive a lower price per unit, shrinking the area of producer surplus below the market price and above the supply curve. Producer surplus decreases.

Statement B (True): At $P_C$: Quantity demanded (QD at $P_C$) > Quantity supplied (QS at $P_C$). This creates a shortage, i.e., excess demand.

Statement C (False): A price ceiling does not create excess supply. It creates excess demand (shortage) because the artificially low price encourages more buying but discourages production. Excess supply (a surplus) results from a price floor set above the equilibrium price.

The false statement is C.

questions.question_text:
The industry is characterized by the following equations:

Total Cost per Firm: TC = 100 + 2Q²
Marginal Cost per Firm: MC = 4Q
Industry Demand Curve: P = 120 - 2Q
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: If there is only one firm (monopoly) in the industry, what is the profit-maximizing quantity and price? Marginal Revenue Curve for the monopolist is given by: MR = 120 - 4Q
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Set MR = MC to find profit-maximizing quantity.
120 - 4Q = 4Q
120 = 8Q
$Q_M$ = 15.

Step 2: Substitute $Q_M$ = 15 into the demand curve to find price.
$P_M$ = 120 - 2(15) = 120 - 30 = 90.

Monopoly equilibrium: $Q_M$ = 15, $P_M$ = 90.

questions.question_text: What is the monopolist's profit at the optimal quantity (Q=15, P=90)?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Calculate Total Revenue at Q = 15, P = 90.
TR = P $\times$ Q = 90 $\times$ 15 = 1,350.

Step 2: Calculate Total Cost at Q = 15.
TC = 100 + 2(15)^2 = 100 + 2(225) = 100 + 450 = 550.

Step 3: Calculate Profit.
$\pi$ = TR - TC = 1,350 - 550 = \$800.

questions.question_text: If the industry is perfectly competitive, what will be the equilibrium quantity and price?
questions.explanation:
In perfect competition, each firm is a price taker and produces where P = MC.

Step 1: Set P = MC.
120 - 2Q = 4Q
120 = 6Q
$Q^* = 20$.

Step 2: Find equilibrium price by substituting $Q^*$ = 20 into the demand curve.
$P^* = 120 - 2(20) = 120 - 40 = 80$.

Competitive equilibrium: $Q^*$ = 20, $P^*$ = 80.

questions.question_text: What is the total profit in perfect competition (at Q=20, P=80)?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Calculate Total Revenue at Q = 20, P = 80.
TR = P $\times$ Q = 80 $\times$ 20 = 1,600.

Step 2: Calculate Total Cost at Q = 20.
TC = 100 + 2(20)^2 = 100 + 2(400) = 100 + 800 = 900.

Step 3: Calculate Profit.
$\pi$ = TR - TC = 1,600 - 900 = \$700.

questions.question_text: What is the social gain (deadweight loss) from moving from monopoly to perfect competition?
questions.explanation:
The Deadweight Loss (DWL) under monopoly is the area of the triangle between the monopoly output and the competitive output.

Key values:
Monopoly: $Q_M$ = 15, $P_M$ = 90.
Competition: $Q^*$ = 20, $P^*$ = 80.

Step 1: Identify the base and height of the DWL triangle.
Base = $Q^* - Q_M$ = 20 - 15 = 5.
Height = $P_M - P^*$ = 90 - 80 = 10.

Step 2: Calculate DWL.
DWL = $\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$ = $\frac{1}{2} \times$ 5 $\times$ 10 = 25.

This represents the value of trades that would have occurred under competition but do not occur under monopoly due to the restricted output.

questions.question_text: The market demand curve for a good is given by: P = 50 - 0.5 Q. If the market price is ₹30, what is the consumer surplus?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Find equilibrium quantity at P = 30.
30 = 50 - 0.5Q
0.5Q = 20
Q = 40.

Step 2: Find the maximum willingness to pay (P-intercept of the demand curve, at Q = 0).
$P_{max}$ = 50.

Step 3: Calculate Consumer Surplus (area of the triangle below the demand curve and above the price).
CS = $\frac{1}{2} \times$ Q $\times$ ($P_{max}$ - P) = $\frac{1}{2} \times$ 40 $\times$ (50 - 30) = $\frac{1}{2} \times$ 40 $\times$ 20 = Rs 400.

questions.question_text: This is the Year 2040. The annual Demand for E-scooters in Bengaluru, driven by generation Z and teenagers of generation Alpha, is given by QD = 5000 - 250P. The quantity is measured in thousands of E-scooters and the price is measured in thousands of rupees per E-scooter. Even though E-scooters are environmentally a better choice, their high-adoption and reckless riding has increased road accidents. As a result, Bengaluru Municipal Corporation (Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike) has imposed a specific (quantity) tax of rupees two thousand per E-scooter (i.e., Rs. 2,000 per E-Scooter) on producers. The before tax supply curve for E-scooters is QS = 600 + 150P. Again, Q is measured in thousands of E-scooters and P is measured in thousands of rupees per E-scooter.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: Find the equilibrium price of E-scooters before the specific tax is levied.
questions.explanation:
Set QD = QS to find equilibrium.
5000 - 250P = 600 + 150P
5000 - 600 = 150P + 250P
4400 = 400P
$P^*$ = 11 (in thousands of rupees) = Rs 11,000.

questions.question_text: Find the equilibrium quantity of E-scooters before the specific tax is levied.
questions.explanation:
Substitute the equilibrium price $P^*$ = 11 into the supply equation.
$Q^*$ = 600 + 150(11) = 600 + 1,650 = 2,250 (in thousands).

Verify using demand: QD = 5000 - 250(11) = 5000 - 2,750 = 2,250. ✓

Equilibrium quantity = 2,250 thousands = 22,50,000 units.

questions.question_text: Find the equilibrium price paid by buyers of E-scooter after the specific tax is levied.
questions.explanation:
A tax of Rs 2,000 = 2 (in thousands) imposed on producers means the seller retains $P_s$ = $P_b$ - 2, where $P_b$ is the buyer's price.

Step 1: Rewrite supply in terms of buyer price.
$Q_S^{new}$ = 600 + 150 $\times$ ($P_b$ - 2).

Step 2: Set QD = $QS^{new}$ and solve for $P_b.$
5000 - $250P_b$ = 600 + 150($P_b$ - 2)
5000 - $250P_b$ = 600 + $150P_b$ - 300
5000 - $250P_b$ = 300 + $150P_b$
4700 = $400P_b$
$P_b$ = 11.75 (thousands) = Rs 11,750.

questions.question_text: Find the equilibrium price earned by the producers of the E-scooters after the specific tax of Rs 2,000 is levied.
questions.explanation:
The tax wedge means: $P_b$ - $P_s$ = T.

The producer receives the buyer's price minus the tax.
$P_s$ = $P_b$ - T = 11,750 - 2,000 = Rs 9,750.

Verification: The tax burden is split as:
- Buyers pay Rs 11,750 vs. pre-tax Rs 11,000: buyer burden = Rs 750.
- Sellers receive Rs 9,750 vs. pre-tax Rs 11,000: seller burden = Rs 1,250.
- Total burden = 750 + 1,250 = Rs 2,000 = the full tax. ✓

questions.question_text: Calculate the fraction of the specific tax that will be passed on to the buyers of E-scooters.
questions.explanation:
Fraction of tax passed to buyers = $\frac{\text{Rise in buyer price}}{\text{Tax amount}}$.

Buyer price before tax: $P_b^{before}$ = Rs 11,000.
Buyer price after tax: $P_b^{after}$ = Rs 11,750.
Tax = Rs 2,000.

Fraction = $\frac{11{,}750 - 11{,}000}{2{,}000} = \frac{750}{2{,}000} = \frac{3}{8}$.

questions.question_text: If a monopoly’s fixed costs increase, its price will _________ and its profit will _________.
questions.explanation:
A monopolist maximizes profit by setting MR = MC.

Key insight: Fixed costs are constant — they do not appear in the MR or MC equations. An increase in fixed costs does not change MR or MC.

Therefore:
- The profit-maximizing quantity $Q^*$ (where MR = MC) is unchanged.
- The price $P^*$ (read from the demand curve at $Q^*$) is unchanged.

However, Total Profit = TR - TC = TR - (VC + FC). Since FC increases, TC increases by the same amount, and profit decreases by exactly the increase in fixed cost.

Result: Price stays the same; profit decreases.

questions.question_text: A competitive firm’s short-run supply curve is its _________ cost curve above its _________ cost curve.
questions.explanation:
A competitive firm is a price taker and maximizes profit by producing where P = MC.

However, the firm only produces if the price covers its average variable cost. The shutdown rule:
- If P < AVC (min): Shut down — the firm cannot even cover variable costs, so it produces zero.
- If P $\geq$ AVC (min): Produce on the MC curve.

Therefore, the short-run supply curve is the marginal cost (MC) curve for all prices at or above the minimum average variable cost (AVC).

The supply curve is: the MC curve above the AVC curve.

questions.question_text: If the cross-price elasticity of demand between two goods is POSITIVE, what does this indicate about their relationship?
questions.explanation:
Cross-price elasticity of demand: $E_{XY} = \frac{\% \Delta Q_X}{\% \Delta P_Y}$.

If $E_{XY}$ > 0: When the price of Y rises, demand for X also rises. Consumers substitute the now-costlier Y with X. The goods are substitutes (e.g., Pepsi and Coca-Cola).

If $E_{XY}$ < 0: When the price of Y rises, demand for X falls. The goods are consumed together — they are complements (e.g., cars and petrol).

If $E_{XY}$ = 0: Changes in the price of Y have no effect on demand for X. The goods are unrelated.

A positive cross-price elasticity indicates the goods are substitutes.

questions.question_text: What is the effect of an increase in the supply of a commodity on equilibrium?

options.A: It leads to a higher equilibrium price and lower equilibrium quantity
options.B: It leads to a lower equilibrium price and higher equilibrium quantity
options.C: It causes no change in equilibrium price or quantity
options.D: It leads to a higher equilibrium price and higher equilibrium quantity

questions.explanation:
An increase in supply means the supply curve shifts rightward.

Step 1: At the original price $P^*$, the rightward shift creates excess supply (QS > QD). There is downward pressure on price.

Step 2: As price falls, quantity demanded increases along the demand curve and quantity supplied decreases along the new supply curve, until a new equilibrium is reached.

New equilibrium:
- Equilibrium price falls: $P^*_{new} < P^*_{old}$.
- Equilibrium quantity rises: $Q^*_{new} > Q^*_{old}$.

An increase in supply leads to a lower equilibrium price and higher equilibrium quantity.

questions.question_text: The demand for water is highly inelastic. If the government imposes a tax on water usage, who will bear most of the tax burden?
questions.explanation:
Tax incidence rule: The more inelastic side of the market bears the larger share of the tax.

Consumer's share of tax = $\frac{E_S}{E_S + |E_D|}$.

For water, demand is highly inelastic ($|E_D| \approx 0$): consumers cannot easily reduce usage (water is a necessity) or switch to alternatives.

As $|E_D| \rightarrow 0$, the consumer's share $\rightarrow \frac{E_S}{E_S + 0} = 1$.

Producers can raise prices almost fully, passing nearly the entire tax on to consumers without losing much quantity sold.

Conclusion: Consumers bear most of the tax burden when demand is highly inelastic.
